newsitem.title: USA: Merger costs hit SBC quarterly results.
newsitem.headline: Merger costs hit SBC quarterly results.

text.p: SBC Communications Inc. reported a net loss of $787 million in the second quarter due mainly to the cost of merging with Pacific Telesis, but its operating results largely matched Wall Street expectations.

The Baby Bell phone company took a charge of $1.6 billion, at the low end of its previously announced range, to cover the costs of its April merger with Pacific Telesis, and to fund various regulatory requirements, it said.

The charges resulted in a net loss of $787 million in the quarter on operating revenues of $5.94 billion, compared with a net income of $803 million on operating revenues of $5.74 billion in the same year-ago period.

Excluding the $1.6 bilion charge, income rose 2.6 percent to $824 million in the period vs. $803 million in the second quarter of 1996. Earnings per share hit 90 cents, a penny below analysts' average forecast and up from 87 cents per share a year ago.
The company said it expected to post $300 million to $500 million in additional charges to cover similar costs during the rest of 1997.
SBC has said revenue growth and cost savings from the merger with Pacific Telesis have the potential to add $1 billion to its bottom line annually by the year 2000.
Annual access line growth was 4.1 percent, driven by 6.2 percent growth in business lines, and 14.5 percent growth in residential additional lines.

Wireless subscribers increased 24.4 percent over the last 12 months to nearly 5 million subscribers, with the addition of 275,000 subscribers during the quarter, one of SBC's strongest-ever quarterly gains, the company said.

SBC Chairman Edward Whitacre said the rollout of its new Personal Communications Services (PCS) -- a new-generation cellular phone service -- in its California and Nevada service areas was running ahead of schedule.
He said its PCS service added 97,000 net new subscribers during the quarter, for a total of 123,000.
"The response to our PCS offering has led us to increase our end-of-year subscriber target to 325,000 subscribers from 250,000," Whitacre said in a statement.

SBC also said it continues to seek entry to the lucrative long-distance market. Earlier this month, the company filed a federal lawsuit challenging certain provisions of the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which prohibits regional Baby Bells from offering long-distance services to their local customers.
SBC's stock fell 94 cents to $59 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
